Figure 1:
StarVector is a foundation model for SVG generation. It uses a Vision-Language Modeling architecture
to understand images and text instructions. StarVector excels at vectorizing a wide range of visual
inputs, from general icons and logotypes to more intricate vectors such as technical diagrams.
StarVector represents a breakthrough in Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) generation, seamlessly integrating visual and textual inputs into a unified foundation SVG model. By reframing vectorization as a code generation task rather than a traditional image processing problem, StarVector transcends previous limitations. This paradigm shift enables the model to leverage the full richness of SVG syntax—including circles, polygons, text elements, and complex paths—without simplification. Our approach allows training on internet-scale data to capture the diverse spectrum of vector representations. At its core, the model employs a vision-language architecture (VLM), enabling unprecedented capabilities in generating complex SVG elements. Complemented by SVG-Stack—our extensive dataset—and SVG-Bench—our comprehensive evaluation framework—StarVector establishes a new paradigm for high-quality vector graphics generation.
Key Capabilities
01
Advanced Multimodal Architecture
StarVector's multimodal architecture processes both visual and textual information with remarkable precision, enabling sophisticated image vectorization and text-guided SVG creation that captures fine details and structural relationships. The image encoder and language decoder work together to understand the semantics of an image in pixel space, recognizing primitive shapes, hierarchies, and layers to produce compact and semantically meaningful SVG primitive outputs.
02
Unparalleled Complexity Handling
Where traditional algorithms falter, StarVector excels—effortlessly recognizing and generating intricate SVG elements including text, complex paths, and various primitives directly from images. The model intelligently identifies geometric shapes, connectivity patterns, and structural elements to produce professional-quality diagrams and icons.
03
Robust Data Foundation
Built upon SVG-Stack—our meticulously curated dataset of over 2 million SVG samples—and evaluated through SVG-Bench, StarVector benefits from diverse, high-quality training examples that ensure consistent performance across various graphic styles and complexities.
04
Leading-Edge Performance
StarVector significantly outperforms existing methods in both text-to-SVG and image-to-SVG generation tasks, demonstrating a substantial leap forward in vectorization quality while remaining fully accessible to the research community as an open-source resource.
Model Architecture
StarVector employs a vision-language architecture to generate high-quality SVG code
Figure 2: a) StarVector Architecture:
StarVector projects images into embeddings via an image encoder,
then maps these embeddings to the LLM hidden space using an LLM Adapter, generating Visual Tokens.
Text conditioning is achieved with the LLM's tokenizer and embedder. The model learns to map token
sequences (visual or textual) to SVG code. The symbol ⊕ denotes mutually exclusive operations (image-to-
SVG or text-to-SVG), while ‖ indicates sequence concatenation.
Figure 2: b)Vision Model and Adapter:
The
image encoder employs a Vision Transformer (ViT) to process image patches sequentially. The LLM Adapter
non-linearly projects embeddings into visual tokens for LLM integration.
The architecture shown above enables StarVector to process both images and text prompts through a unified framework. This approach allows the model to leverage the strengths of both modalities, resulting in more accurate and contextually appropriate SVG generation. The LLM Adapter is a critical component that bridges the gap between visual and textual representations, ensuring that the model can effectively translate visual information into structured SVG code.

data.title: Collapse OS
data.author: kaycebasques
data.article_summary: Collapse OS是一款旨在应对文明崩溃后技术恢复的操作系统。它基于Forth语言，包含工具和文档，目标是在资源匮乏的环境下仍能对微控制器进行编程。系统设计注重简易性和自给自足，能够在自制、拼凑的机器上运行，通过简易接口进行操作，编辑文本和二进制内容，编译多种微控制器和处理器的汇编代码，读写多种存储设备，并能够自我构建和部署。主要特征包括支持Z80、8086、6809和6502等处理器，具备命令行和视觉化文本编辑器，以及二进制编辑功能。整个项目代码少于2000行，可在POSIX环境下用简单工具构建。项目代码托管于SourceHut，由Virgil Dupras主导开发。文中还提及了相关的技术复兴项目。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：关于在社会可能崩溃的情况下，使用和制造简易计算机及电子设备的可行性和优先级

不同观点：
• [palmotea] 认为在可能的社会崩溃前，关注制造简易计算机项目只是娱乐性质的活动（LARPing），而不是实际有用的准备。他质疑这些项目在崩溃场景下的实际价值，并指出像农耕手册这样的实际准备可能更有用。

• [barbequeer] 提到自己曾经认为有关文明崩溃的讨论是荒谬的，但随着看到一些合理的观点，开始反思自己是否低估了这种可能性。他认为提出“在什么条件下文明会崩溃”以及“文明持续存在的必要条件”是有趣且值得思考的问题。

• [alnwlsn] 分享了自己在设计和使用简易Z80计算机方面的经验，并认为在某些情况下，其他技术可能比微控制器更适合使用，尤其是机械定时器等更易于 improvised 的设备。

• [jeffchien] 提出希望有一个指南来帮助识别可能含有兼容微处理器的机器，并讨论了在某些场景下寻找这些设备的可能性。他还提到了现代芯片如ESP32s和Arduinos可能在某些末日场景中难以获取。

• [apitman] 以幽默的方式批评了网站使用简单的HTTP/1.1协议，暗示项目在技术实现上的简陋。

• [foenix] 提到自己在2010年就曾提出类似问题，并指出讨论在15年间的变化，反映了对这一话题的长期兴趣。

• [vdupras] 提供了额外的网站链接以防当前网站超负荷，并提到新链接还未完全切换，显示了对技术资源可用性的实际考虑。

• [panarchy] 强调了使用低技术工具组装电子部件的重要性，并引用了有关“通孔安装类型”的讨论，同时也提到了使用表面安装技术的可能性，如clay PCBs。

• [generalizations] 认为在崩溃后，设计一个能将各种电力转换为12v直流电的变压器，并配合纸质手册指导如何发电和使用铜线等材料，比单纯依赖数字工具更实际。

• [phendrenad2] 以幽默的方式问项目是否能在IBM 5100上运行，暗示对老旧设备兼容性的关注。

补充讨论：
• 争议的焦点在于这些简易计算机项目在社会崩溃场景下的实际价值，以及哪些技术和设备才是最优先和实用的准备。
• 讨论中还涉及了不同技术在崩溃场景下的可行性和易用性，如机械定时器与微控制器的对比，以及不同类型芯片的可用性。
• 对技术资源在崩溃后的可持续性和可获取性也进行了讨论，包括如何在资源有限的情况下设计和使用电子设备。

43482705.article_content:
Collapse OS
Bootstrap post-collapse technology
Winter is coming
and Collapse OS aims to soften the blow.  It is a
Forth
(why Forth?)
operating system and a collection of tools and
documentation with a single purpose: preserve the ability to program
microcontrollers through
civilizational collapse
. It is designed to:
Run on minimal and improvised machines.
Interface through improvised means (serial, keyboard, display).
Edit text and binary contents.
Compile assembler source for a wide range of MCUs and CPUs.
Read and write from a wide range of storage devices.
Assemble itself and deploy to another machine.
Additionally, the goal of this project is to be as self-contained as possible.
With a copy of this project, a capable and
creative
person should
be able to manage to build and install Collapse OS without external resources
(i.e.  internet) on a machine of her design, built from scavenged parts with
low-tech tools.
Features
Runs on Z80, 8086, 6809 and 6502 machines with very little resources.
Can assemble Z80, AVR, 8086, 6809 and 6502 binaries.
Can disassemble 6502 and 6809.
Can program AVR microcontrollers.
Has a command line text editor similar to Forth's traditional editor as
well as a visual text editor inspired by UNIX' VI.
Has a visual binary editor.
Has the full power of a reasonably well-featured Forth interpreter.
Can be built from a POSIX environment with minimal tooling: only cc and
make are needed.
Excluding machine-specific ports, less than 2000 lines of code.
Getting Collapse OS
The code of collapse OS is available as a
git repo on SourceHut
. Refer
to instructions in README.
Funding
You are inspired by Collapse OS and would like to fund its development? I don't
do any kind of crowdfunding, but if you happen to be a rich philanthropist,
maybe we can do something.
Discussion
My name is Virgil Dupras and I can be reached at hsoft@hardcoded.net.
There's also
Dusk OS' mailing list
Related efforts
Here is a list of related efforts that I find noteworthy:
Dusk OS
Tumble Forth
Public Domain Books to Restart Computer Technology
Civboot: a civilizational bootstrapper
Simplifier
Sci.Electronics.Repair FAQ
The Vintage Technology Digital Archive
A big collection of Apple-related documentation
Daniel Marks' electronic designs focusing on resilience
Michael Schierl's UXN port of Collapse OS
Deadly Optimism, Useful Pessimism

data.title: Microsoft Study: AI Makes Human Cognition "Atrophied and Unprepared"
data.author: greybox
data.article_summary: 微软和卡内基梅隆大学的一项研究发现，随着人们在工作中越来越依赖生成式人工智能，他们的批判性思维使用减少，可能导致认知能力退化。研究人员指出，自动化剥夺了人们处理常规任务的机会，使其在面对例外情况时缺乏判断力和准备。研究招募了319名知识工作者，他们 self-reported 了936个使用生成式AI的实例。调查显示，过度依赖AI工具可能导致用户对自己完成任务的能力信心下降，例如教师用DALL-E生成图片、交易员用ChatGPT提升技能、护士验证AI生成的教育手册等。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：AI对人类认知能力的影响，尤其是在解决问题和理解系统方面。

不同观点：
• [gatinsama] 认为理解系统的工作原理是无法委派给他人的，尤其是对于复杂的项目，理解和决策系统的运作方式是最困难的部分。如果不理解系统，就无法知道它是否按预期工作。
• [vunderba] 指出，过度依赖像ChatGPT这样的工具会削弱人们的批判性思维能力。这种依赖使得人们失去了培养内在有价值技能的机会，而这种技能只能通过刻意的练习来提高。将LLM与计算器的发明相比较是不恰当的，因为计算器是用来辅助解决更大问题的。
• [lenerdenator] 表示，AI像Google搜索一样，使信息的记忆成为可选的认知负担，而人们通常会抛弃这种负担。不过，个人的认知问题不一定需要AI来造成萎缩和 unprepared。
• [masfuerte] 认为这种现象并不是新的，早在1990年代银行员工的工作自动化时就出现了类似的情况。随着软件处理例外情况的能力增强，员工的技能逐渐萎缩，处理更难例外的能力下降。
• [sollewitt] 提出，LLM可以在语言学习中发挥积极作用，提供“认知健身房”的效果。LLM可以提供灵活的对话和解释，超越Duolingo等工具的局限性。
• [greybox] 引用微软的研究指出，自动化可能导致人类认知的萎缩和 unprepared，因为剥夺了人们在日常任务中锻炼判断力的机会。
• [0x20cowboy] 分享个人经验，承认在疲劳或烦躁时会过度依赖LLM，直接复制错误信息而不加思考，这种行为让他感到自己的认知能力下降，但同时有一种奇怪的满足感。
• [piltdownman] 提到使用AI需要额外的“合成思维努力”来引导AI响应，这可能增加认知负担。有人认为，这种“合成思维努力”可以作为评估AI使用成本/收益的关键绩效指标。
• [deadbabe] 认为，发展中国家的儿童由于缺乏AI工具，必须依靠自己的脑力解决问题，从而可能获得超越发达国家儿童的机会。对发达国家儿童的描述则较为负面。
• [moralestapia] 认同认知能力下降的观点，特别是在COVID后教育水平下降的背景下。同时认为能够正确推理的人类会变得更加有价值。

补充讨论：
• 争议焦点在于AI工具对人类认知能力的影响，尤其是对批判性思维和问题解决能力的潜在削弱。
• 一些人认为AI可以作为有效的学习工具，提供传统方法无法比拟的优势，如语言学习中的灵活对话。
• 微软的研究被多次引用，以支持关于自动化导致认知萎缩的讨论。
• 对发达国家和发展中国家儿童的对比讨论，引发了对AI工具普及不均可能导致教育机会不平等的担忧。

总体来看，讨论围绕AI对人类认知的双重影响展开，既有对潜在负面影响的担忧，也有对其作为学习工具的积极评价。

The researchers recruited 319 knowledge workers for the study, who self reported 936 first-hand examples of using generative AI in their job, and asked them to complete a survey about how they use generative AI (including what tools and prompts), how confident they are the generative AI tools’ ability to do the specific work task, how confident they are in evaluating the AI’s output, and how confident they are in their abilities in completing the same work task without the AI tool. Some tasks cited in the paper include a teacher using the AI image generator DALL-E to create images for a presentation about hand washing at school, a commodities trader using ChatGPT to “generate recommendations for new resources and strategies to explore to hone my trading skills,” and a nurse who “verified a ChatGPT-generated educational pamphlet for newly diagnosed diabetic patients.”

data.title: Ratomic: Provides Mutable data structures for use with Ruby's Ractors
data.author: ksec
data.article_summary: Ratomic 是一个提供可变数据结构的 Ruby 库，专为 Ruby 的 Ractors 设计，使其能够突破 GVL（全局解释器锁）的限制，实现更好的扩展性。该项目包含几个 Ractor 安全的数据结构，如计数器（Counter）、对象池（Pool）、映射（Map）和队列（Queue）。这些结构的 API 相对有限，主要用于类级别的常量，可以被多个 Ractors 共享。目前项目还在初期阶段，特别欢迎熟悉 Rust 和 Ruby C 扩展的开发者贡献代码。Ratomic 采用 MIT 许可协议。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：Ractors在Ruby中实现可共享数据结构的潜力及相关技术细节

不同观点：
• jeremy_k认为Jean的文章详细讨论了在Ruby中实现Ractor可共享数据结构的必要性，特别是提到需要一些基本的数据结构如Ractor::Queue和Ractor::ConcurrentMap，以便在Ractors中运行完整的应用程序。他还指出C扩展需要支持可移动类型。jeremy_k承认自己尚未深入研究Ractors的具体使用，但对相关讨论的增加感到鼓舞。

• rco8786对Ractor-safe数据结构库的开发表示兴奋，并提到自己之前在相关文章中看到这个想法，并留下了评论。他对这个想法迅速变为现实感到惊喜。

补充讨论：
• jeremy_k和rco8786都提到了具体的数据结构如Queue和Map在Ractors中的实现，表明这些数据结构在支持Ractor应用中的重要性。
• rco8786的评论显示出对社区讨论和实际开发进展的关注，表明社区对Ractors技术发展的积极参与和支持。
• 尽管两人都对Ractors的发展表示乐观，但jeremy_k坦言自己尚未完全理解所有技术细节，这表明在社区中可能存在对Ractors复杂性的认知差距。

争议焦点：
• 目前没有明显的争议，但jeremy_k对技术细节的部分理解不清可能反映了更广泛的社区对Ractors及其应用的认知和学习曲线问题。

Ratomic
Ratomic provides mutable data structures for use with Ruby's Ractors.
This allows Ruby code to scale beyond the infamous GVL.
HELP WANTED!
If you know Rust and Ruby C-extensions, we need your help!
This project is brand new and could use your knowledge!
If you don't know Rust or C, consider this a challenge to learn and solve.
Read through the
issues
to find work that sounds interesting to you.
Installation
Install the gem and add to the application's Gemfile by executing:
bundle add ratomic
TODO: We have not released a gem yet.

Ratomic provides several useful Ractor-safe structures.
Note the APIs available are frequently very limited compared to Ruby's broad API.

data.title: AI will change the world but not in the way you think
data.author: tlhunter
data.article_summary: 文章讨论了大型语言模型（LLMs）对社会、教育和商业交流的影响。LLMs虽无法推理或预测未来，但能从训练数据中提取趋势并生成各种文本。在教育领域，LLMs引发了学校对作弊的恐慌，因为学生可以利用这些工具轻松完成作业。然而，文章质疑这种恐慌是否必要，并提出反思传统作业形式的必要性。在商业交流中，LLMs帮助简化和自动化繁琐的电子邮件写作，将冗长的信息压缩成简洁的要点。文章指出，这种技术虽然起初看似神奇，但随着普及可能变得平常。最终，LLMs正在改变我们沟通和完成任务的方式，促使我们重新思考语言和交流的效率。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：AI生成内容、简洁表达（如 bullet points）与详细叙述的优劣，以及其对沟通和工作的影响。

不同观点：
• **Proggy**：认为作者过于强调简洁表达，忽略了叙述中的“冗余”在提供背景、情感表达和人类故事讲述中的重要性。Proggy 进一步指出，现代信息过载问题不能通过单纯去除冗余来解决，而应通过限制信息的质量流入来应对。
  
• **Palmotea**：部分同意作者的观点，但提醒不应过度泛化。认为有些“冗余”可能是必要的，尤其是在复杂的思想表达中。同时批评部分软件工程师可能因为自认为“聪明”而忽视了这一点。

• **Dkdcwashere**：认为作者用大量文字表达简单观点是一种讽刺，支持去除不必要的冗长叙述，尤其是在商业环境中，更高效的沟通会成为趋势。

• **Gioazzi**：支持使用LLM（大型语言模型）作为审核工具而非写作者，认为这种方法能够保持沟通的有效性。

• **Jonnycat**：通过对比bullet points和长篇叙述的效果，质疑作者是否真的认为所有内容都可以压缩成简洁形式，认为不同形式有不同的沟通效果。

• **Irrational**：质疑商业沟通中的“客套话”是否必要，认为直接切入主题更有效，尤其在编程世界中，这种“客套话”并不常见。

• **The_bear**：认为LLM将短提示扩展为长代码块并不等同于商业邮件中的无意义冗余，因为代码需要零解释空间，而自然语言则需要一定的冗余来避免误解。

• **Neilv**：反对使用AI生成的信息，认为这样做会丧失个人表达的独特性和信息传递的精确性。

• **Bobek**：同意AI生成内容导致沟通效率降低的现象，并认为需要远离此类沟通方式，回归真正的沟通者。

• **Wheelie_boy**：不认为编程语言的讨论适用于作者的观点，指出不同编程语言和开发过程中的多样性需求。

• **Bsenftner**：从更广泛的社会角度讨论AI的影响，认为AI将大幅提高知识工作者的工作难度和要求，迫使人们熟练使用AI以保持竞争力。

43483011.article_content:
AI will change the world but not in the way you think
On the inevitable evolution of business speak and programming languages
6 min read
Mar 19, 2025
Support this website by purchasing prints of my photographs! Check them out here.
The current generation of consumer facing AI tools, known as Large Language Models (LLMs), continue to proliferate through society, used by folks from every stage of life, from office workers to school children. At a high level these tools are trained on a large collection of text-based content (such as every webpage on the internet and every book ever published; hard to get much larger than that) and sometimes further trained for a given industry (such as medical research, industrial design, law, etc.)
While it's true that LLMs are unable to reason or predict the future they are able to extract trends from the information they are trained on and they are able to output everything from bullet lists to essays to data that is easily parsed by computer programs.
Science fiction author Arthur C. Clarke once said that "Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic." It's true that nascent technology is exciting, particularly when encountered for the first time. I recall my first ride in a self-driving car. Like all technology it proliferates society and adoption increases and before you know it light bulbs and radio are ubiquitously boring.
When LLMs first appeared schools went into full panic mode. Suddenly a middle schooler could type "write a three page book report about moby dick" into a prompt and paste the result into a Google Doc, print it out, and turn it in. Schools banned the technology and some sought tools to "detect AI writing," which turned out to be as accurate as flipping a coin.
Was such panic deserved? Possibly. The point of a book report is to test if a student read the required material and was able to comprehend what it was about and the use of an LLM tool defeated this test. That said, is it a beneficial assignment to ask a student to read a long book? I haven't a clue. Is it beneficial to ask a student to write an essay? More on that in a moment.
LLMs affect the business world as well. But let's take a step back. How are professionals expected to communicate with each other? Usually with empty platitudes to kick things off like "Hey! How's it going? How's the family? How are you doing?" Messages are expected to be written across several coherent English sentences, neatly organized into paragraphs, finally with some sort of signature. In the programming world we refer to this as boilerplate.
What is it that we are really trying to communicate? Usually a few short ideas that could be represented as bullet points, but that we need to fluff up with meaningless words so that we don't sound rude. Of course, this changes by culture and by language and is not applicable to many parts of the world, but it is definitely a thing in American English.
So now we see interactions with LLM tools that look a little like this:
HUMAN PROMPT:
Please write a professional and courteous email based on these topics:
Joe's code quality is poor
Joe needs to refactor his work instead of publishing Pull Requests so quickly
Joe needs to stop annoying people to rush a review and merge his PRs
I recommend Joe reads a copy of the book Code Complete
LLM RESPONSE:
Subject: Feedback on Code Quality and Development Practices
Hi Joe,
I appreciate the effort youâve been putting into your work and your enthusiasm for getting changes merged quickly. I wanted to share some feedback that I believe will help improve the overall quality of your contributions.
I've noticed that some of your recent pull requests could benefit from additional refinement before submission. Rather than pushing PRs too quickly, taking more time to refactor and review your code internally can lead to higher-quality changes and smoother reviews. This will also help reduce the need for rushed feedback and rework later on.
Additionally, Iâd like to encourage a more patient approach to the review process. While itâs great to be proactive, giving reviewers adequate time ensures a more thorough and thoughtful review, ultimately leading to better outcomes.
To further support your growth as a developer, I highly recommend reading Code Complete by Steve McConnell. It provides excellent insights into writing clean, maintainable, and well-structured code. I think youâll find it valuable in refining your approach.
Let me know if you'd like to discuss any of this in more detailâIâd be happy to help.
Best,
{Your Name}
Of course, we're all busy, not only those who write email, but those who read it as well. So what does Joe do? He visits his friendly local LLM, of course.
HUMAN PROMPT:
Please convert the following long email from a colleague into a few bullet points:
Hi Joe,
â¦
Best,
Thomas
LLM RESPONSE:
Appreciate your enthusiasm and effort in getting changes merged quickly.
Suggest taking more time to refi

data.title: What Killed Innovation?
data.author: speckx
data.article_summary: 文章探讨了数据可视化领域的创新停滞问题。作者回顾了2012年D3.js出现后，互动图形和实验项目蓬勃发展的时期，当时每个新项目都在推动数据可视化的边界。然而，十年后的今天，作者感到许多作品变得千篇一律，缺乏新意。通过与业界专家的讨论，文章提出了几个可能的原因：新闻编辑室的数字化奠定了早期实验基础，但如今视觉风格更加同质化，模板化和软件默认设置普遍。商业方面，对独立数据可视化项目的投资减少。作者还指出两个关键变化：一是“滚动叙述”（scrollytelling）的普及，虽然初期令人兴奋，但很快成为标准；二是互动图形的创新速度放缓。文章总结，当前的创意陷入了一种“高原期”，需要新的突破。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：数据可视化领域的创新与实用性之间的平衡

不同观点：
• **实用性优先**：[janalsncm] 认为，数据可视化的核心目的是让人们容易理解数据。频繁改变可视化方式会增加理解难度，有时简单的条形图就是最佳选择。复杂和创新的可视化虽然有趣，但不一定实用。
• **创新周期论**：[0xbadcafebee] 提出，创新往往以爆发形式出现，并在人类需求减少或研发遇到瓶颈时停滞。虽然对当前的网络平台持批评态度，但对未来的技术创新仍抱有希望，认为原生应用可以提供更多可能性。
• **数据素养与欺骗性**：[praptak] 指出，数据素养让人对复杂可视化持怀疑态度。图表如饼图和颜色选择不当可能误导观众，因此复杂的创新可视化可能增加误解风险。
• **过度创新与疲劳**：[Ragnarork] 质疑不断创新可视化方式的必要性，认为创新应以实用为前提，而不是为了创新而创新。过度复杂的可视化会增加解读难度，不利于普及。
• **经济回报与创新**：[fullshark] 提到，创新网络可视化的经济回报不高，除非能引发病毒式传播。简单的煽动性言论可能比复杂的可视化更具吸引力。
• **技术演进与创新减少**：[jeffreyrogers] 认为，数据可视化领域创新减少是因为我们已经找到了解决大多数问题的标准方法。历史上的印刷可视化也呈现类似模式。

补充讨论：
• **具体案例批评**：[ralferoo] 对"512 paths to the white house"图表表示困惑，认为复杂且不直观，不如英国的简单清晰方法有效。
• **技术疲劳与专业工具**：[Animats] 提到专业人员使用的工具（如Bloomberg终端）通常视觉上不吸引人但功能实用，反映出对复杂可视化的疲劳感。
• **视觉印象与实际帮助**：[Avshalom] 指出，一些视觉上 impressive 的可视化实际上并不实用。
• **法律与市场限制**：[jmclnx] 认为，大公司通过法律和市场手段限制创新，导致小公司难以生存，从而减少了创新活力。
• **数据与智慧的区别**：[jrm4] 强调，漂亮的数据不等于信息或智慧，可能只是“数据色情”，没有实际价值。
• **技术进化与AI的影响**：[lmeyerov] 认为，数据可视化并没有消亡，而是在进化。AI和生成式AI正在改变可视化的应用方式，使得可视化不再是目标，而是过程的一部分，最终目标是提供答案和自动化。

争议焦点：
• 创新的必要性与实用性之间的平衡：一方认为不断创新可视化方式能带来更好的理解，另一方则认为过度复杂化会增加理解难度，应以实用为主。
• 复杂可视化的实际效用：一些人质疑复杂可视化是否真正有助于理解数据，还是只是视觉上吸引人但实际效果有限。

Mar 05, 2025
This is part of a trilogy on the state of our industry:
Part 1:
Outside a clientâs comfort zone
Part 2:
What killed innovation? A brief history
Part 3: (Coming soon)
I entered the data visualization field in 2012, when D3.js had just come out and interactive graphics were going through a digital Renaissance.  By the time I was fully steeped in the field in 2016, it felt like a new, experimental project was coming out every weekâeach one pushing the boundaries of how we think about, visualize, and communicate data.
New York Times'
512 Paths to the White House
from 2012.  When I think of the pre-scrollytelling era, it's always the first one I point to.
But fast forward a decade, and it feels like Iâm seeing the same polished but predictable formats over and over.
At first, I thought I had gotten jaded (a decade in tech feels like forever and maybe Iâm now just the old granny shaking my fist about the âgood old daysâ ð), but after talking to a few friends and mulling on it for a couple years, I now have some hypotheses on how we might have gotten here.
To test these hypotheses, I asked a few very respected voices in our industryâall known for their beautiful, bespoke work and responsible for driving the field forward in one way or another.  So Iâd like to thank everyone who kindly contributed: Nadieh Bremer, Giorgia Lupi, Federica Fragapane, Caitlin Ralph, Matt Daniels, RJ Andrews, Alberto Cairo, Eric William Lin, and Moritz Stefaner. While some of them are quoted directly, all of them provided insightful and nuanced answers that helped to shape my own whirlwind of ideas about where we are today, how we got here, and where weâre headed.
A brief history (of a plateau)
Let me come out swinging: our industryâs creativity has plateaued.
Ok, I donât fully mean that (but itâs got a lot of potential for a click-bait title, no? ð).  Let me provide a bit more nuance: the craft of telling data-informed stories on the web has plateaued.
As Alberto recounts, newsrooms started digitizing in the mid-to-late 1990s, and by the time I started in the early 2010s, the foundations were laid out for really interesting web-based experiments.  It was the perfect storm: Javascript was maturing, browser performance was improving, and D3.js was releasing interesting new layouts and supporting chart-specific interactions every year.  I was constantly coming across new chart forms, and new ways to add interactions and animations to layer information.  Just look at these two New York Times pieces from 2012 and 2013:
Four Ways to Slice Obamaâs 2013 Budget Proposal
(2012, left) and
Among the Oscar Contenders, a Host of Connections
(2013, right).  From a technical perspective, I remember being so mind-blown about how the different budget items animated so smoothly between the different views, and so inspired by the use of force-directed graph to lay out the Oscar nominees (and that visual elegance!).
It really seemed like no two data visualizations looked the same.
RJ agrees that web interactives âhit some kind of romantic peakâ in the mid-to-late 2010s.  Nadieh dreamily recalls the advent of D3 visuals like chord diagrams and circle packing. âI canât tell you what other mind boggling new technique or technology since then has, Iâve felt, made an impact,â she laments. âAnd that makes me very sad.â
Moritz summarizes his recent observations with the precision and insight of an industry veteran who has put out inspiration after inspiration for decades:
The few viral, well-known data visualizations tend to be static images or movies or small, personalized apps rather than elaborate interactive web pieces.
Visual styles are more homogenous,  with many projects looking similar due to the prevalence of established formats, templated solutions and software defaults.
On the commercial side, investments in bespoke data visualization from freelancers and independent studios have declined.
Moritz has written a whole blog post in response, with the most amazing title:
âWhy 2024 was a dead year for indie dataviz â and how weâll do much better in 2025â
.  Itâs well worth a thorough read.
He declares: âitâs a polycrisisâ.
But how did we get here (polycrisis)?
Over the past decade, Iâve noticed two fundamental shifts that have changed how we design interactive graphics on the web.
The first: scrollies.
I still remember when I first saw Stephanie Yee and Tony Chuâs
âA visual introduction to machine learningâ
in 2016, I was blown away:
It felt so exciting that web performance had come so far, that browsers could continuously scroll
and
animate thousands of elements at the same time. Scrollytelling was so quickly adopted that there was even a big debate about whether scrollies or steppers were âbetterâ (beautifully summarized
in this blog post
by Zan Armstrong). But the scrolly won out

data.article_summary: Google DeepMind推出Gemini 2.5，这是其最智能的AI模型。Gemini 2.5 Pro Experimental在多项基准测试中领先，尤其在推理和编码能力方面表现突出。该模型具备“思考”能力，能在回应前进行推理，提高准确性和性能。Gemini 2.5 Pro在数学和科学基准测试中表现优异，并在编码任务中展现强大能力，例如创建网页应用和编辑代码。该模型拥有1百万token的上下文窗口（即将扩展至2百万），能处理多种数据类型。开发者可在Google AI Studio和Gemini app中试用该模型，后续将登陆Vertex AI平台。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：Gemini 2.5模型的性能和应用

不同观点：
• **[og_kalu]** 认为Gemini 2.5在长篇小说写作中表现出色，特别是解决了LLM在故事细节处理上的"神经质"问题，例如不合理的故事节奏。但他也指出，为了达到正常的故事节奏，需要生成大量内容，这在以前是不需要的。
• **[malisper]** 使用数学谜题测试Gemini 2.5，发现其数学推理能力超过了95%的人口，并能迅速解决复杂问题，显示出模型的强大推理能力。
• **[simonw]** 对Gemini 2.5在音频转录、时间戳和图像识别方面的表现印象深刻，并指出其在绘制图像任务中的优秀表现。
• **[freediver]** 认为Gemini 2.5在基准测试中表现优异，质量高且精准，但速度稍慢。
• **[anotherpaulg]** 强调Gemini 2.5在编码竞赛中的领先表现，尤其是在多语言编程任务中。
• **[Oras]** 对持续的"最先进模型"声明和基准比较感到麻木，认为这些宣传缺乏新意，降低了兴奋感。
• **[mindwok]** 通过调试Dart库代码的案例，展示了Gemini 2.5在识别和修复代码错误方面的突破性能力。
• **[greatgib]** 提醒用户注意Google的使用条款，警告不要输入机密信息，因为这些信息可能会被用于改进Google的产品和服务。
• **[jnd0]** 对Gemini 2.5的智能表现和联网功能感到满意，并期待其支持更多功能，如画布模式。
• **[jorl17]** 分享了在分析大量诗歌文本上的突破性体验，认为这是第一次能自信地将大量数据推理任务交给LLM模型。
• **[vineyardmike]** 对模型的命名方式提出质疑，认为*.5的命名可能只是市场营销手段，缺乏实际意义。
• **[zone411]** 提供了Gemini 2.5在NYT Connections基准测试中的具体分数，显示其相对于其他模型的显著改进。
• **[falcor84]** 对Gemini 2.5在Aider Polyglot编码任务中的快速进步表示赞赏，并期待其在ARCGI 2任务中的表现。
• **[nickandbro]** 测试了Gemini 2.5在绘制图像任务中的表现，对其准确生成指定图像的能力感到惊讶。

补充讨论：
• **隐私和数据安全**：[greatgib] 提到了使用LLM模型时的隐私问题，强调用户应注意不要输入敏感信息。
• **模型命名争议**：[vineyardmike] 对*.5命名方式表示不满，认为这是市场营销的结果，建议采用更合理的命名方式。
• **市场竞争**：多位评论者提到了Gemini 2.5在不同基准测试和任务中的领先表现，显示出其在市场中的竞争力。

争议焦点：
• **模型的命名方式**：部分用户对*.5命名方式感到困惑和不满，认为这是市场营销策略，而非技术进步的标志。
• **隐私问题**：用户对模型使用过程中涉及的隐私条款表示关注，担心数据被用于改进产品。

总结：Gemini 2.5在多种任务中表现出色，特别是在长文本处理、数学推理和编码任务中。然而，用户对其命名方式和隐私条款存在一定争议。

43473489.article_content:
Gemini 2.5: Our most intelligent AI model
Mar 25, 2025
·
[[read-time]] min read
Share
Twitter
Facebook
LinkedIn
Mail
Copy link
Gemini 2.5 is a thinking model, designed to tackle increasingly complex problems. Our first 2.5 model, Gemini 2.5 Pro Experimental, leads common benchmarks by meaningful margins and showcases strong reasoning and code capabilities.
Koray Kavukcuoglu
CTO of Google DeepMind
Share
Twitter
Facebook
LinkedIn
Mail
Copy link
Today we’re introducing Gemini 2.5, our most intelligent AI model. Our first 2.5 release is an experimental version of 2.5 Pro, which is state-of-the-art on a wide range of benchmarks and debuts at #1 on
LMArena
by a significant margin.
Gemini 2.5 models
are thinking models, capable of reasoning through their thoughts before responding, resulting in enhanced performance and improved accuracy.
In the field of AI, a system’s capacity for “reasoning” refers to more than just classification and prediction. It refers to its ability to analyze information, draw logical conclusions, incorporate context and nuance, and make informed decisions.
For a long time, we’ve explored ways of making AI smarter and more capable of reasoning through techniques like
reinforcement learning
and
chain-of-thought prompting
. Building on this, we recently introduced our first thinking model,
Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking
.
Now, with Gemini 2.5, we've achieved a new level of performance by combining a significantly enhanced base model with improved post-training. Going forward, we’re building these thinking capabilities directly into all of our models, so they can handle more complex problems and support even more capable, context-aware agents.
Introducing Gemini 2.5 Pro
Gemini 2.5 Pro Experimental is our most advanced model for complex tasks. It tops the
LMArena
leaderboard — which measures human preferences — by a significant margin, indicating a highly capable model equipped with high-quality style. 2.5 Pro also shows strong reasoning and code capabilities, leading on common coding, math and science benchmarks.
Gemini 2.5 Pro is available now in
Google AI Studio
and in the
Gemini app
for Gemini Advanced users, and will be coming to
Vertex AI
soon. We’ll also introduce pricing in the coming weeks, enabling people to use 2.5 Pro with higher rate limits for scaled production use.
Enhanced reasoning
Gemini 2.5 Pro is state-of-the-art across a range of benchmarks requiring advanced reasoning. Without test-time techniques that increase cost, like majority voting, 2.5 Pro leads in math and science benchmarks like GPQA and AIME 2025.
It also scores a state-of-the-art 18.8% across models without tool use on Humanity’s Last Exam, a dataset designed by hundreds of subject matter experts to capture the human frontier of knowledge and reasoning.
Advanced coding
We’ve been focused on coding performance, and with Gemini 2.5 we’ve achieved a big leap over 2.0 — with more improvements to come. 2.5 Pro excels at creating visually compelling web apps and agentic code applications, along with code transformation and editing. On SWE-Bench Verified, the industry standard for agentic code evals, Gemini 2.5 Pro scores 63.8% with a custom agent setup.
Here’s an example of how 2.5 Pro can use its reasoning capabilities to create a video game by producing the executable code from a single line prompt.
Building on the best of Gemini
Gemini 2.5 builds on what makes Gemini models great — native multimodality and a long context window. 2.5 Pro ships today with a 1 million token context window (2 million coming soon), with strong performance that improves over previous generations. It can comprehend vast datasets and handle complex problems from different information sources, including text, audio, images, video and even entire code repositories.
Developers and enterprises can start experimenting with Gemini 2.5 Pro in
Google AI Studio
now, and
Gemini Advanced
users can select it in the model dropdown on desktop and mobile. It will be available on
Vertex AI
in the coming weeks.
As always, we welcome feedback so we can continue to improve Gemini’s impressive new abilities at a rapid pace, all with the goal of making our AI more helpful.

How Elon Musk’s SpaceX Secretly Allows Investment From China
by
Joshua Kaplan
and
Justin Elliott
March 26, 2025, 6 a.m. EDT
As a U.S. military contractor, SpaceX sees allowing Chinese ownership as fraught. But it will allow the investment if it comes through secrecy hubs like the Cayman Islands, court records say. “It is certainly a policy of obfuscation,” an expert said.
by
Joshua Kaplan
and
Justin Elliott
March 26, 2025, 6 a.m. EDT
Share
Contrast
Change Appearance
Change Appearance
Auto
Light
Dark
Republish
ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up to receive
our biggest stories
as soon as they’re published.
Elon Musk’s aerospace giant SpaceX allows investors from China to buy stakes in the company as long as the funds are routed through the Cayman Islands or other offshore secrecy hubs, according to previously unreported court records.
The rare picture of SpaceX’s approach recently emerged in an under-the-radar corporate dispute in Delaware. Both SpaceX’s chief financial officer and Iqbaljit Kahlon, a major investor, were forced to testify in the case.
In December, Kahlon testified that SpaceX prefers to avoid investors from China because it is a defense contractor. There is a major exception though, he said: SpaceX finds it “acceptable” for Chinese investors to buy into the company through offshore vehicles.
“The primary mechanism is that those investors would come through intermediate entities that they would create or others would create,” Kahlon said. “Typically they would set up BVI structures or Cayman structures or Hong Kong structures and various other ones,” he added, using the acronym for the British Virgin Islands. Offshore vehicles are often used to keep investors anonymous.
Experts called SpaceX’s approach unusual, saying they were troubled by the possibility that a defense contractor would take active steps to conceal foreign ownership interests.
Kahlon, who has long been close to the company’s leadership, has said he owns billions of dollars of SpaceX stock. His investment firm also acts as a middleman, raising money from investors to buy highly sought SpaceX shares. He has routed money from China through the Caribbean to buy stakes in SpaceX multiple times, according to the court filings.
The legal dispute centers on an aborted 2021 deal, when SpaceX executives grew angry after news broke that a Chinese firm was going to buy $50 million of the company’s stock. SpaceX then had the purchase canceled. In separate testimony, the rocket company’s CFO explained that the media coverage was “not helpful for our company as a government contractor.” SpaceX’s business is built on those contracts, with the U.S. government paying the company billions to handle sensitive work like building a classified spy satellite network.
Get in Touch
Do you have any information we should know about Elon Musk’s businesses? Josh Kaplan can be reached by email at
[email protected]
and by Signal or WhatsApp at 734-834-9383. Justin Elliott can be reached by email at

and by Signal or WhatsApp at 774-826-6240.
Company executives were concerned that coverage of the deal could lead to problems with national security regulators in the U.S., according to Kahlon’s testimony and a filing from his attorneys.
SpaceX, which also launches rockets for NASA and sells satellite internet service, is perhaps the most important pillar of Musk’s fortune. His
estimated 42% stake
in the company is valued at around $150 billion. If he owned nothing else, he’d still be richer than Bill Gates.
Federal law gives regulators broad power to oversee foreign investments in tech companies and defense contractors. Companies only have to proactively report Chinese investments in limited circumstances, and there aren’t hard and fast rules for how much is too much. However, the government can initiate investigations and then block or reverse transactions they deem a national security threat. That authority typically does not apply to purely passive investments in which a foreign investor is buying only a small slice of a company. But experts said that federal officials regularly ask companies to add up Chinese investments into an aggregate total.
The
U.S. government charges
that China has a systematic strategy of using even minority investments to secure leverage over companies in sensitive industries, as well as to gain privileged access to information about cutting-edge technology. U.S. regulators view even private investors in China as potential agents of the country’s government, experts said.
The new materials do not contain allegations that the Chinese investments in SpaceX would violate the law or were directed by the Chinese government. The company did not respond to detailed questions from ProPublica. Kahlon declined to comment on the reasons for SpaceX’s approach.

data.title: Why is C the symbol for the speed of light? (2004)
data.author: fanf2
data.article_summary: 本文讨论了为什么用字母 **c** 作为光速的符号。尽管19世纪常用 **V** 表示光速，但1856年韦伯和Kohlrausch在一篇论文中使用 **c** 表示一个电动力学常数，后来被证明与光速有关。1894年，Paul Drude将 **c** 用于表示电动力学波的速度。随着马克斯·普朗克和洛伦兹等物理学家的采用，**c** 逐渐成为光速的标准符号。1907年，爱因斯坦也在论文中改用 **c**。虽然韦伯最初用 **c** 表示“常数”（constant），但拉丁语中 **celeritas** 意为“速度”，这可能是 **c** 最终被用来表示光速的原因。爱因斯坦曾在1905年使用 **V**，但1907年后改用 **c**。自相对论书籍开始出版以来，几乎无一例外地使用 **c** 作为光速的符号。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：符号 _c_ 作为光速或因果速度的表示的起源和意义

不同观点：
• [技术解释] xenadu02 认为 _c_ 是因果速度，光的传播速度是其结果，而非原因。光子由于无质量，以空间维度中的最大速度移动，从光子的视角看，穿越宇宙是瞬时的。
• [符号纠正] throwawayk7h 指出标题中的符号应为小写的 _c_ 而不是大写的 _C_。
• [词源讨论] fsckboy 提到 _c_ 来自拉丁语 "celeritas" 意为速度，并指出 "celerity" 在描述波动传播速度时仍被使用。
• [幽默/文化引用] tonymet 开玩笑说 _C_ 代表 "Cochranes"，引用自虚构人物 Zefram Cochrane。
• [传统解释] hangonhn 提到自己学到的是 _c_ 代表常数（constant），并认为这个解释听起来合理，但承认未仔细考证。
• [猜测] wnissen 猜测 _c_ 是发现过程中一个临时的符号，并指出科学发现过程往往比后来描述的更复杂。
• [幽默/双关] smallmouth 开玩笑说 _c_ 代表光是因为光是辐射谱中唯一能被看见的部分。
• [历史解释] pyuser583 认为 _c_ 最初代表洛伦兹常数（Lorenz Constant），而非光速。
• [定义区分] rakoo 试图区分 "speed" 和 "celerity"，认为前者适用于有质量的物体，而后者用于无质量的信息传递。

补充讨论：
• [无关讨论] gnarlynarwhal42 提到当地学校和植物园，偏离主题。
• [无关链接] simonjanssen 分享了一个与测量有关的玩笑视频链接。
• [参考之前讨论] nhatcher 提供了之前相关讨论的链接。
• [编程幽默] Surac 作为程序员开玩笑说 _c_ 是快速构造一个完整 bogus 程序的方式。
• [幽默回应] WaNumberLookup 对问题表示有趣。
• [技术幽默] DarkNova6 开玩笑说因为 C++ 还没被发明，所以用 _c_ 表示光速。

争议焦点：
• 符号 _c_ 的真正含义和起源：不同评论者提供了技术、词源、传统和历史等多种解释，反映了对同一符号的多角度理解和误解。

43472663.article_content:
[Physics FAQ]
-
[Copyright]
By Philip Gibbs, 1997, 2004.
Why is
c
the symbol for the speed of light?
"As for
c
, that is the speed of light in vacuum, and if you ask why
c
,
the answer is that it is the initial letter of
celeritas
, the Latin word meaning
speed." Isaac Asimov in "C for
Celeritas
(1959)" [1]
A Short Answer
Although
c
is now the universal symbol for the speed of light, the most common
symbol in the nineteenth century was an upper-case
V
which Maxwell had started
using in 1865.  That was the notation adopted by Einstein for his first few papers on
relativity from 1905.  The origins of the letter
c
being used for the speed of
light can be traced back to a paper of 1856 by Weber and Kohlrausch [2].  They
defined and measured a quantity denoted by
c
that they used in an electrodynamics
force law equation.  It became known as Weber's constant and was later shown to have
a theoretical value equal to the speed of light times the square root of two.  In
1894 Paul Drude modified the usage of Weber's constant so that the letter
c
became
the symbol for the speed of electrodynamic waves [3].  In optics Drude continued to
follow Maxwell in using an upper-case
V
for the speed of light.  Progressively
the
c
notation was used for the speed of light in all contexts as it was picked up
by Max Planck, Hendrik Lorentz and other influential physicists.  By 1907 when
Einstein switched from
V
to
c
in his papers, it had become the standard
symbol for the speed of light in vacuum for electrodynamics, optics, thermodynamics and
relativity.
Weber apparently meant
c
to stand for "constant" in his force law, but there is
evidence that physicists such as Lorentz and Einstein were accustomed to a common
convention that
c
could be used as a variable for velocity.  This usage can be
traced back to the classic Latin texts in which
c
stood for "celeritas" meaning
"speed".  The uncommon English word "celerity" is still used when referring to the
speed of wave propagation in fluids.  The same Latin root is found in more familiar
words such as acceleration and even celebrity, a word used when fame comes quickly.
Although the
c
symbol was adapted from Weber's constant, it was probably thought
appropriate for it to represent the velocity of light later on because of this Latin
interpretation.  So history provides an ambiguous answer to the question "Why is
c
the symbol for the speed of light?", and it is reasonable to think of
c
as
standing for either "constant" or "celeritas".
The Long Answer
In 1992 Scott Chase wrote on sci.physics that "anyone who read hundreds of books by
Isaac Asimov knows that the Latin word for `speed' is `celeritas', hence the symbol `c'
for the speed of light".  Asimov had written an article entitled "C for Celeritas" in
a sci-fi magazine in 1959 and had reprinted it in some of his later books [1].  Scott
was the first editor of the Physics FAQ on Usenet and Asimov's explanation was later

43472663.article_summary: 本文讨论了为什么用字母 **c** 作为光速的符号。尽管19世纪常用 **V** 表示光速，但1856年韦伯和Kohlrausch在一篇论文中使用 **c** 表示一个电动力学常数，后来被证明与光速有关。1894年，Paul Drude将 **c** 用于表示电动力学波的速度。随着马克斯·普朗克和洛伦兹等物理学家的采用，**c** 逐渐成为光速的标准符号。1907年，爱因斯坦也在论文中改用 **c**。虽然韦伯最初用 **c** 表示“常数”（constant），但拉丁语中 **celeritas** 意为“速度”，这可能是 **c** 最终被用来表示光速的原因。爱因斯坦曾在1905年使用 **V**，但1907年后改用 **c**。自相对论书籍开始出版以来，几乎无一例外地使用 **c** 作为光速的符号。
43472663.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：符号 _c_ 作为光速或因果速度的表示的起源和意义

不同观点：
• [技术解释] xenadu02 认为 _c_ 是因果速度，光的传播速度是其结果，而非原因。光子由于无质量，以空间维度中的最大速度移动，从光子的视角看，穿越宇宙是瞬时的。
• [符号纠正] throwawayk7h 指出标题中的符号应为小写的 _c_ 而不是大写的 _C_。
• [词源讨论] fsckboy 提到 _c_ 来自拉丁语 "celeritas" 意为速度，并指出 "celerity" 在描述波动传播速度时仍被使用。
• [幽默/文化引用] tonymet 开玩笑说 _C_ 代表 "Cochranes"，引用自虚构人物 Zefram Cochrane。
• [传统解释] hangonhn 提到自己学到的是 _c_ 代表常数（constant），并认为这个解释听起来合理，但承认未仔细考证。
• [猜测] wnissen 猜测 _c_ 是发现过程中一个临时的符号，并指出科学发现过程往往比后来描述的更复杂。
• [幽默/双关] smallmouth 开玩笑说 _c_ 代表光是因为光是辐射谱中唯一能被看见的部分。
• [历史解释] pyuser583 认为 _c_ 最初代表洛伦兹常数（Lorenz Constant），而非光速。
• [定义区分] rakoo 试图区分 "speed" 和 "celerity"，认为前者适用于有质量的物体，而后者用于无质量的信息传递。

补充讨论：
• [无关讨论] gnarlynarwhal42 提到当地学校和植物园，偏离主题。
• [无关链接] simonjanssen 分享了一个与测量有关的玩笑视频链接。
• [参考之前讨论] nhatcher 提供了之前相关讨论的链接。
• [编程幽默] Surac 作为程序员开玩笑说 _c_ 是快速构造一个完整 bogus 程序的方式。
• [幽默回应] WaNumberLookup 对问题表示有趣。
• [技术幽默] DarkNova6 开玩笑说因为 C++ 还没被发明，所以用 _c_ 表示光速。

争议焦点：
• 符号 _c_ 的真正含义和起源：不同评论者提供了技术、词源、传统和历史等多种解释，反映了对同一符号的多角度理解和误解。

data.author: aizk
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕AI技术、职业转型、技术开发及其相关问题的讨论

不同观点：
• [Jdfmiller] 认为AI导致失业在未来会成为严重问题，但目前过度悲观无助于事，应该积极面对并采取行动。同时分享了LLM（如ChatGPT）在代码编写中的帮助，但强调背景知识仍至关重要。
• [lwansbrough] 讨论了技术项目的开发，指出作者在描述其项目时显得有些自我中心，并分享了自己在类似项目中的不同技术选择和经历。虽然自己的项目耗时更长且未发布，但赞赏原作者的快速完成。
• [timkq] 提出LLM让非软件工程师也能开发技术产品，但质疑这些产品在长期维护和技术债务方面的可持续性。
• [janalsncm] 对“随机算法”提出不同看法，认为“随机”只是算法的一种形式，适用于探索阶段，但用户最终会希望根据已有经验进行选择，而不是持续随机。

• [wonger_] 提到自己容易被新闻骗局欺骗，特别是在睡眠不足的情况下，涉及信息真实性和警惕性的问题。
• [bradleykingz] 对诈骗行为的荒谬性表示震惊，提到一个关于“无法停止放屁的狗”的骗局，暗示网络上存在许多荒唐的诈骗手段。

• 主要体现在[lwansbrough]对[原作者项目描述]的质疑，认为其描述显得自我中心，暗示自己可能被认为是抄袭了类似想法。
• [timkq]对LLM赋能非技术人员开发产品的长期可行性的担忧，可能暗示这些产品在技术维护上的不足。

data.title: Brain scans of infants reveal the moment we start making memories
data.author: Brajeshwar
data.article_summary: 这篇文章讨论了一项新研究，旨在揭示为何人们无法记住生命最初三年的记忆，即“婴儿期遗忘”现象。通过使用功能性磁共振成像（fMRI）扫描26名4至25个月大的婴儿和幼儿的大脑，研究团队发现，大约在一岁时，大脑中的海马体开始活跃，并生成与记忆相关的神经信号。尽管婴儿在这一时期学习语言、走路和建立社交关系，但他们成年后却无法回忆起这些早期记忆。研究表明，婴儿能够形成短暂的记忆，但可能由于海马体尚未发育成熟，这些记忆无法长久保存。该研究帮助科学家理解记忆形成和遗忘的机制。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：婴儿记忆的形成与遗忘原因，及其与大脑发育的关系

不同观点：
• CarRamrod认为，记忆的编码、长期存储和回忆这三个步骤中的任何一步失败都会导致遗忘。然而，由于婴儿在MRI机器中乱动，目前难以确定具体是哪个步骤导致婴儿记忆的丧失。他还表达了对过度简化科学内容的 clickbait 式文章的不满。

• bildung 指出，早期记忆的形成困难主要是因为大脑在快速重塑，但学习并非“混乱”，而是非常泛化的。尽管海马体在18-24个月才开始发育，但人们在此之前已经开始学习。婴儿时期的学习更多是泛化的，而非情景性的。

• drooby 和 hnpolicestate 分享了自己早期记忆的个人经历，并表示这些记忆经过与父母的确认，具有一定的真实性。这表明有些人确实保留了非常早期的记忆，尽管这种现象可能较为罕见。

• locallost 提到自己的孩子在3岁时能够记住一年前的事情，但随着年龄增长出现了记忆的“断层”，这与孩子大脑发育的阶段性变化有关。

• hereme888 支持了一项基于 spaced-repetition 算法的研究，指出7岁以下儿童的记忆力较差是因为他们的脑力集中在神经重塑上。

• SwtCyber 对未来研究寄予希望，认为未来可能会进一步揭示记忆巩固与睡眠之间的关系。

• dwighttk 对脑成像研究的可靠性持怀疑态度，认为科学研究可能需要经过多次修正才能得出较为准确的结论，类似于古生物学家拼接恐龙骨骼的过程。

• ofrzeta 对脑成像结果持谨慎态度，认为虽然扫描提供了一些有趣的线索，但未来研究可能会进一步揭示支持生动自传体记忆的脑结构基础。

• sidewndr46 以讽刺的语气质疑脑成像故事的实际意义，暗示这类研究可能缺乏实际应用价值，类似于研究鳟鱼何时开始形成记忆。

补充讨论：
• 争议的焦点之一在于婴儿记忆的形成时间与遗忘原因。有些人认为早期记忆是泛化的，而非情景性的，而其他人则基于个人经验认为有些早期记忆是具体而生动的。
• 另一个值得注意的讨论点是对脑成像研究结果的不同态度，一些人对其抱有希望，而另一些人则持怀疑态度，认为这些研究可能需要经过多次修正才能得出可靠结论。

43437725.article_content:
Science
Brain Scans of Infants Reveal the Moment We Start Making Memories
Kids form fleeting memories at around 12 months, even as their brains are rapidly rewiring themselves.
Shelly Fan
Mar 20, 2025
Image Credit
Juan Encalada on Unsplash
Share
A giggling toddler in a pink dress and matching headphones lies down on her back in front of a gigantic whirling machine. A pillowy headrest cushions her head. She seems unfazed as she’s slowly shuttled into the claustrophobic brain scanner. Once settled, a projection showing kaleidoscope-like animations holds her attention as the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machine scans her brain.
The girl is part of
a new study
seeking to answer a century-old mystery: Why can’t most us remember the first three years of our lives? Dubbed “infantile amnesia” by Sigmund Freud, the study could provide insight into how the brain develops during our early years. And if we can form memories at a young age, are they fleeting, or are they still buried somewhere in the adult brain?
It seems like a simple question, but an answer has eluded scientists.
Though infants and toddlers aren’t yet able to give detailed verbal feedback, studying their behavior has begun to shed light on if and when they remember people, things, or places. Still, the approach can’t peek in on what’s happening in the brain in those early years. MRI can.
A team from Columbia and Yale University scanned the brains of 26 infants and toddlers aged 4 to 25 months as they completed a memory task. They found that at roughly a year old, a part of the brain crucial to memory formation spun into action and began generating neural signals related to things the kids remembered from the tests.
Called the hippocampus, this sea-horse-shaped structure deep inside the brain is crucial to the encoding of our life stories—who, when, where, what. Adults with a damaged hippocampus suffer memory problems. But because wiring inside the hippocampus is still developing during our earliest years, scientists believe it may be too immature to form memories.
“It’s not that we don’t have any memories from that period [infancy],” said study author Nicholas Turk-Browne in a press briefing. “In fact, early life is when we learn our language. It’s when we learn how to walk…learn the names of objects and form social relationships.”
“What happens during that period when we learn so much, but remember so little?” he added.
Stages of Memory
Memory seems like all-or-none: You either remember something, or you don’t.
It’s not that simple. Decades of research have identified the hippocampus as the main orchestrator of episodic memories. These allow you to remember an acquaintance at a party, where you parked your car, or what you had for dinner three nights ago.
Each everyday experience is encoded in
neural connections
in the hippocampus. Groups of neurons called engrams capture different memories and keep them separate, so that they don’t bleed into each other.
Once encoded, the brain
etches important memories into long-term storage during sleep
. Studies of slumbering rodents and humans after learning a new task found that the hippocampus replayed brain activity at higher speed during the night, correlating with better performance on a trained memory task the next day.
The last step is retrieval. This is when the brain fishes out stored memories and delivers them to our conscious brain—and so, we “remember.”
Failure of any of these steps causes amnesia. So, which steps are responsible for the erosion of baby memories?
Bundles of Joy
Brain scans from 26 infants now offer some intriguing clues.
The team behind the new study scanned the children’s brains with functional MRI (fMRI) as they looked at a screen in the scanner and took a memory test. fMRI captures brain oxygen levels (BOLD) as a proxy for local neuron signaling—higher levels mean more brain activity.
The head needs to keep very still throughout the scans to avoid blurring. That’s not easily accomplished with babies and toddlers. Previous studies circumvented the problem by imaging their brains while sleeping, but the results couldn’t capture memory processes.

To keep the infants happy, engaged, and safe, parents brought favorite blankets and pacifiers, and younger infants were wrapped inside a comfortable vacuum pillow to reduce movement. A video system projected images onto the ceiling of the scanner within their line of sight.
As the kids looked at a bright kaleidoscope-like video, images of faces, scenes, and objects would flash for a few seconds. These included toys or landscapes of an alpine cabin with mountains in the background. Previous studies found infants like to stare at objects or images they’ve seen before compared to new objects, suggesting they remember previous encounters.

data.title: Does all intelligent life face a Great Filter?
data.author: xweb
data.article_summary:
这篇文章讲述了著名的“费米悖论”的起源和相关理论。1950年左右，UFO热潮引发了对外星飞行器可能性的广泛讨论。物理学家恩里科·费米在一次与同事的午餐讨论中突然提出了一个问题：“大家都在哪儿呢！？”这成为了费米悖论的核心，即如果宇宙中存在大量智慧文明，为什么我们没有看到任何证据？

文章进一步介绍了罗宾·汉森提出的“大过滤器”理论，试图解释这个悖论。该理论认为，在生命发展到星际探索阶段的过程中，可能存在一个不可避免的障碍，导致智慧文明极为罕见。如果这个过滤器在我们后面，说明我们是幸运的幸存者；如果在我们前面，则预示着人类未来可能面临重大挑战。

总之，费米悖论揭示了我们对智慧生命普遍性的假设可能存在错误，而大过滤器理论提供了一种可能的解释。

主要讨论点：人类文明在崩溃后的恢复能力，以及历史上与现代文明在灾难情景下的应对差异。

不同观点：
• [bell-cot的观点]
  - 历史上，人类文明不需要遭遇彻底的灾难就能崩溃。适度的压力（如轻微的局部气候变化或资源枯竭）或几代人的富裕生活导致的 complacency 都可能导致文明崩溃。
  - 崩溃的原因通常是短视和缺乏远见。
  - 前1800年的技术条件下，文明即使完全崩溃，幸存者也能较快重建，因为大多数人口是自给自足的农民，拥有必要的技能和知识来维持或重建文明。
  - 现代文明在全面崩溃的情况下会表现得更糟，因为关键基础设施的供应链是全球性的，重建文明需要成千上万的专家。

• [yawpitch的观点]
  - 对上述观点持怀疑或调侃态度，表示如果有机会遇到“崩溃后重建文明的人”，会询问他们的看法。

补充讨论：
- [bell-cot] 强调历史上的文明崩溃往往源于短视和资源管理不善，而不一定是巨大的灾难。
- [bell-cot] 指出前1800年技术条件下的文明具有较强的自我恢复能力，因为人口主要为自给自足的农民，技能和知识分布较为集中。
- [bell-cot] 进一步指出，现代文明由于全球化供应链和高度专业化的知识结构，在面对全面崩溃时将更加脆弱。
- [yawpitch] 对整个讨论持怀疑态度，可能认为这种讨论过于理论化或不切实际。

争议焦点：
- 现代文明与历史文明在面对崩溃时的应对能力和恢复速度的差异。

“Where is everybody!?”
It was around 1950. UFO mania had recently ramped up across the world, with dozens of reported sightings of strange flying machines fueling rampant speculation regarding their origins.
The eminent physicist Enrico Fermi was visiting his colleagues at Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico that summer, and the mealtime conversation turned to the subject of UFOs. Very quickly, the assembled physicists realized that if UFOs were alien machines, that meant it was possible to travel faster than the speed of light. Otherwise, those alien craft would have never made it here.
At first, Fermi boisterously participated in the conversation, offering his usual keen insights. But soon, he fell silent, withdrawing into his own ruminations. The conversation drifted to other subjects, but Fermi stayed quiet.
Sometime later, long after the group had largely forgotten about the issue of UFOs, Fermi sat up and blurted out: “But where is everybody!?”
Every scientist at that table immediately knew what he meant.
That central question—where is everybody?—is now known as the Fermi Paradox in his honor. And while he wasn't the first person to wonder about the nature of other intelligent civilizations, he was the first to give the idea a modern spin.
The paradox arises from a seemingly innocent line of rational thinking that leads to an incorrect conclusion. It goes like this. We’re not special. We live on just another rocky planet around a ho-hum star in an unspectacular arm of an average spiral galaxy. There’s nothing incredibly unique or exotic about our physical circumstances.
And here we are. Alive. Intelligent. (Almost) spacefaring.
Nature tends not to do things just once. If we’re here and on the cusp of exploding into space, and there are hundreds of billions of stars in the galaxy, trillions of galaxies in the Universe, and billions of years to play around with, the Universe should be teeming with alien civilizations. We should see evidence for them everywhere we look, the same way we see any other common process played out again and again in the cosmos.
And yet we’ve got nothing. No artificial signals in our radio receivers. No mega-engineering projects reshaping other solar systems. No artifacts embedded in our planet or any others. As far as we can tell, we are alone. To the limits of our observations, we are the only living creatures, the only intelligent civilization, to inhabit the cosmos.
So what gives? Something must be wrong with the chain of reasoning. Even though every step sounds sane and reasonable, it leads to a conclusion that flies in the face of the evidence. Hence, a paradox.
Doomsaying with Robin
Decades later, the economist Robin Hanson was mulling over Fermi’s paradox and came to an uncomfortable conclusion. Maybe we’re alone because essentially nobody ever makes it. Maybe there’s some unavoidable barrier between the origin of intelligent life and said life setting off to explore the galaxy.
The position of this Great Filter, as he named it, is critically important as we contemplate the future of humanity. If the Filter is behind us, in our past, then we are one of the few lucky ones to survive in an otherwise lonely universe. If it’s in front of us, in our future, then we likely do not have much time left as a species (at least, a spacefaring one).
The key point of the Great Filter argument is that Fermi’s Paradox is not really a paradox. Instead, there is a false assumption baked into the chain of reasoning. The assumption is that because life is probably common, intelligent, spacefaring life is also common. Take that assumption away and Fermi’s argument breaks down, resolving the paradox. But how do we square the claim that intelligent life is rare with the solid argument that there’s nothing special happening here on Earth?
It comes down to a game of numbers. Intelligent life doesn’t have to be outright impossible. In fact, it can’t be—we’re here, and we’ve already begun taking our first steps into space. It just has to be so deeply rare that we shouldn’t expect to see any evidence for it elsewhere, despite decades of searching. So the game is to start with the plausible assumption of abundant life, then find a way to whittle that down to as close to zero as we can get it.
Hanson pointed out that life requires many steps to reach spacefaring status—especially the kind of spacefaring status that would get you noticed by nascent astronomers across the Universe. First off, life needs a place to call home. As far as we know, that means a rocky world with lots of liquid water, a decent atmosphere, and a stable star.
Second, life has to… well, become alive. There’s some secret sauce that turns an odd collection of prebiotic compounds and molecules into self-reproducing structures that undergo Darwinian evolution.

data.title: Search My Site – open-source search engine for personal and independent websites
data.author: OuterVale
data.article_summary: searchmysite.net是一个专注于“独立网络”或“小型网络”的搜索引擎，收录个人和独立网站的非商业内容。其特点包括：仅索引用户提交和审核的网站，避免垃圾信息和过度优化的内容；无广告，以减少垃圾信息和监视资本主义的激励；通过“搜索即服务”功能维持运营，不依赖广告；提供高度隐私保护，不收集个人信息；完全开源，增加透明度和社区参与。该搜索引擎适合寻找个人经验和深度研究主题的用户。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：复古和个人网站搜索引擎的推荐与评价

不同观点：
• OuterVale：介绍了Wiby搜索引擎，强调其索引要求，包括页面设计简洁、非商业化、少用脚本和CSS、避免侵入式广告以及不作为其他网站的门户。
• danlitt：推荐了Marginalia搜索引擎，并引用了之前的讨论链接。
• renegat0x0：列举了多个相关网站，如Nownow, Omg.lol等，并分享了自己的爬虫项目和个人网页数据库。
• rumgewieselt：喜欢Pagefind.app的简洁设计。
• kreelman：质疑Postgres数据库对于个人网站搜索工具是否过于庞大，但对更多此类工具的出现表示欢迎。
• 1dom：对发现随机但经过深思熟虑的个人网站表示赞赏，认为这些网站使网络更加伟大。
• unfixed：认为这类项目非常适合发现有趣的博客和 obscure 网站，个人首选Marginalia搜索引擎。
• _puk：认为现代网络搜索被污染，广告和技巧繁多，导致优质内容难以被发现。期待无广告、注重结构化数据的搜索引擎。
• ThinkBeat：对LLM模型在搜索引擎中的作用表示困惑。
• nelsonfigueroa：喜欢任何能帮助发现新个人网站和博客的工具。
• saltysalt：推荐自己创建的Greppr.org。
• aleken：认为该工具正是自己寻找的，但对需要使用Postgres数据库表示惊讶。
• csprimer-in：不理解该搜索引擎与其他搜索引擎的区别，请求帮助理解。
• eviks：指出该搜索引擎缺乏基本的拼写纠错功能。
• tobiasnvdw：立即发现了一个之前从未见过的新博客，表示赞赏。

补充讨论：
• 搜索引擎的功能和设计简洁性是讨论的核心，许多评论者对简洁和非商业化的页面表示赞赏。
• 争议焦点在于使用Postgres数据库的必要性，部分评论者认为对于个人网站搜索工具来说过于复杂。
• 不同搜索引擎如Wiby和Marginalia被多次提及，用户对它们的评价和推荐也是讨论的重点。
• 有评论者对LLM模型在搜索引擎中的具体作用感到困惑，显示出对新技术整合的理解差异。
• 发现新博客和个人网站的价值被广泛认可，显示出用户对早期互联网体验的怀旧和对优质内容的追求。

About searchmysite.net
What is the search engine and why should I use it?
The searchmysite.net search engine is a niche search, focussing on the "indieweb" or "small web" or "digital gardens", i.e. non-commercial content, primarily personal and independent websites.
If you want to research people's personal experiences of or deep-dives into certain topics, hobbies or interests, then you may find the searchmysite.net public search useful to avoid having to wade through all the marketing websites and blog spam that fill the big search engines. It differs from the commercial search engines because it:
Indexes only user-submitted and moderated sites, rather than indexing the entire internet with all of its spam, "search engine optimisation" and "click-bait" content.
Does not show adverts and promotes advert-free results pages, to remove the incentives for spam and surveillance capitalism.
Aims to have a sustainable and user-aligned operating model, planning to pay running costs via the "search as a service" features, rather than relying on advertising which could put it in conflict with user needs.
Offers an unusually high level of privacy for a search engine, thanks to the operating model which is not based on advertising or collecting personal information for sale to advertisers (see the Privacy Policy for full details).
Is fully open source, for even greater transparency of the searching, ranking and indexing processes, and for greater community involvement in improving the service.
